papers.title_in_file: Grover Speedup from Many Forms of the Zeno Effect
papers.version_note: arXiv:2305.11146v5, 15 Nov 2024; the text layer carries the journal version (Quantum, accepted 2024-11-04). Equations and square roots are partly garbled in the text layer. Page numbers in anchors are the printed page numbers of this copy.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper (with numerical illustrations) that argues three families of analog mechanisms (phase rotation, dephasing and measurement, destruction of the excited state), each with Zeno-effect manifestations, can reach the optimal square-root-of-N unstructured-search scaling in a single avoided crossing model.

assertions.value: The authors state that Zeno effects from measurement, decoherence, and decay of the excited state into a computationally useless state can each support an optimal Grover-like speedup on unstructured search in a direct analog setting.
quotes: In this paper we show that they can support such a speedup, whether due to measurement, decoherence, or even decay of the excited state into a computationally useless state.
are able to support an optimal quantum speedup for unstructured search.
assertions.certainty_reason: The result rests on scaling arguments in a two-state model plus numerical illustrations, not on a theorem with stated conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is for the idealised single avoided crossing model, not for a full many-qubit Hamiltonian.

assertions.value: The authors group the algorithms into three families: one based on phase kicks (adiabatic computation and continuous-time quantum walks), one based on dephasing and measurement, and one based on destruction of amplitude within the excited state.
quotes: one based on phase kicks, containing adiabatic computation and continuous-time quantum walks; one based on dephasing and measurement; and finally one based on destruction of the amplitude within the excited state
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own organisation of the families in the abstract and Section 2.2.

assertions.value: The authors define a Zeno effect as any interaction that prevents a quantum system from entering a state by interfering with the buildup of coherences, which are the off-diagonal elements of a density matrix. They define Zeno dynamics as the possibly trivial dynamics of a system confined by Zeno effects.
quotes: by Zeno effect, we mean any interaction which prevents a quantum system from entering a state by interfering with buildup of coherences, which can be expressed mathematically as the off-diagonal elements of a density matrix.
by Zeno dynamics, we mean the (possibly trivial) dynamics of a system which is confined by Zeno effects.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the definition for its own use in Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors limit the study to a speedup on unstructured search, because the best known scaling is known there and so an advantage can be proven. They state that this differs from combinatorial optimisation, where the best classical scaling is not known.
quotes: In this manuscript, we focus on a speedup on unstructured search. The advantage of this setting, is that the scaling of the best known possible algorithm is known, so an advantage can be proven.
This contrasts with combinatorial optimisation problems, where the best classical scaling is not known.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that real optimisation problems have structure that should not be ignored, and that performance on unstructured search only indicates whether quantum superposition could hypothetically give an advantage.
quotes: While real optimisation problems of interest have structure which should not be ignored, performance on unstructured search can give an indication whether it is hypothetically possible to use quantum superposition to gain an advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own results in Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors report that, for every mechanism they examine, the models can reach the theoretically optimal square-root-of-N speedup, matching the scaling of Grover's original algorithm.
quotes: all models can reach the theoretically optimal N speedup, matching the scaling of the original algorithm by Grover [36, 37].
assertions.certainty_reason: Shown by scaling arguments and numerics in a two-state model; the printed square root sign is lost in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer drops the square root sign before N; the surrounding text and Section 2.2 confirm the intended scaling is the square root.

assertions.value: The authors state that if dephasing or dissipation could be done in constant time independent of system size, unstructured search of any size would take the same time. They state that such a result can only come from an unrealistic description of a physical system.
quotes: if we assume that dephasing or dissipation can be accomplished in constant time, independent of the size of the system, then this would lead to a system where unstructured search of any size can be accomplished in the same amount of time.
Such a result can only come from an unrealistic description of a physical system
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the timescale constraint it imposes on every channel it models.

assertions.value: The authors state that any physical quantum system can be efficiently simulated by a universal quantum computer, and cite Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani [53] for the proof that such computers cannot exceed the Grover square-root-of-N scaling.
quotes: and it has been proven that such computers cannot exceed the N scaling of Grover’s algorithm [53].
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result; the paper does not re-prove it.

assertions.value: The authors state that a major contribution is to show that, for the models they examine, physically realistic versions are able to achieve, but not exceed, the square-root-of-N scaling.
quotes: A major contribution of the current work is to show
that for the models we examine, physically realistic versions are able to achieve (but not exceed)
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about the paper's own contribution, supported by arguments rather than a theorem.

assertions.value: The authors build on the single avoided crossing model, a two-level model introduced in earlier work by other authors. They state it covers unstructured search for transverse field (hypercube) and complete graph drivers, and that the optimal annealing schedule in it is the cotangent of pi times the scaled time.
quotes: This work builds on a model of unstructured search known as the single avoided crossing model.

This model is relevant to a wide variety of cases of unstructured search, including all computationally relevant qudit models, and for both transverse field (aka hypercube) and complete graph drivers.
Within the single avoided crossing model, an optimal annealing schedule is defined as
f (τ ) = cot(πτ ).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the model it uses for all later results.

assertions.value: The authors argue that using the schedule with diverging energy scale instead of a realistic cutoff version gives a population error of order inverse N, no larger than the error already accepted by ignoring random guessing of the answer.
quotes: This suggests further that the error in the populations from using f (τ ) instead of the more realistic f¯(τ ) will be of O(N −1), which is no larger than the level of error we have already implicitly accepted from
assertions.certainty_reason: A perturbative argument stated with 'suggests', not a proved bound.

assertions.value: The authors state a three-step recipe for an optimal speedup: identify a quantum channel whose timescale is proportional to the inverse instantaneous gap; build a protocol that stays mathematically identical when the product of runtime and minimum gap is held fixed; verify a non-zero probability of finding the marked state from the start state in the single avoided crossing model.
quotes: Identify an implementation of a quantum channel where the relevant timescale is proportional to g−1(τ )
Develop a protocol consisting of a series of implementations of this channel which remains mathematically identical as long as T gmin is held fixed.
Verify that the protocol has a non-zero probability of finding |m⟩ starting from |ω˜⟩ within the single avoided crossing model.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own method in Section 2.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that runtime scaling slower than the inverse gap would beat the known optimal Grover speedup and so could only come from an unphysical channel. They state that scaling faster than the inverse gap but slower than its inverse square is a non-optimal speedup, and that inverse-square scaling gives overall scaling of N, the best classical scaling.
quotes: Any scaling which is slower than g−1(τ ) would correspond to a speedup
better than the known optimal (Grover) speedup, and therefore could only come about from a quantum channel which is somehow unphysical
A quantum channel where the runtime scales as g−2(τ ) would result in an overall algorithmic scaling of N , which is the best classical scaling.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument by classification in the paper, not a proof with stated conditions.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as far as they are aware, algorithms based on moving amplitude from the excited state to a computationally useless state have not previously been explored in the literature.
quotes: As far as we are aware, this is a class of algorithms which have not previously been explored in the literature.
assertions.certainty_reason: A novelty claim by the authors, with no search shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that computation driven by dissipation from the excited state into the ground state is not addressed in this work, because it cannot be considered a source of a Zeno effect.
quotes: an important topic, but not one which we address in the present work because it cannot be considered a source of a Zeno effect.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this exclusion from its own scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that a quantum walk at the avoided crossing, or within a fixed finite multiple of the minimum gap of it, always attains an optimal speedup, but this requires exponentially increasing precision.
quotes: A quantum walk at exactly the avoided crossing or within a fixed finite multiple of gmin of the avoided crossing will always attain an optimal quantum speedup, but this requires exponentially increasing precision.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a consequence of the model without a formal proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that a finite number of quantum-walk stages still gives an optimal speedup, outside a pathological set of cases of measure zero where the final probability of the marked state is exactly zero.
quotes: an optimal speedup would still occur, outside of a pathological set of cases of measure zero where the final probability of |m⟩ is exactly zero.
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued from non-zero final overlap, not proved as a theorem.

assertions.value: The authors report from their plots that, for a fixed runtime with tscale ≤ π and no noise, a multi-stage quantum walk is superior to the adiabatic protocol in absolute performance, consistent with reference [42]. They report that the decrease is monotonic.
quotes: These show that for a fixed runtime where tscale ≤ π and no noise, a quantum walk is superior
to adiabatic in terms of absolute performance, consistent with the findings of [42].
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from numerical plots in the idealised model.

assertions.value: The authors argue that, as the number of stages grows, a fixed fraction of the protocol time is spent where the eigenstates overlap both the uniform superposition and the marked state, so the marked state probability is non-zero apart from special runtimes with perfect destructive interference. They conclude these protocols give an optimal Grover speedup.
quotes: This proves that with the possible exceptions of special cases, these protocols will give optimal Grover speedup as well.
with the possible exception of special runtimes where perfect destructive interference could occur.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors call it a proof but the argument is qualitative and exceptions are not bounded.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper uses the word proves for a qualitative non-vanishing argument; no theorem with explicit conditions is stated.

assertions.value: The authors state that a schedule need only have finite f for a finite fraction of the scaled time, and avoid exact destructive interference, to give an optimal speedup. They state that the crucial ingredient is the correct scaling around the avoided crossing as the problem grows.
quotes: such a schedule need only have f (τ ) finite for a finite fraction of τ values, and to avoid special cases where exact destructive interference could occur.
The crucial ingredient for optimal speedup is for the schedule to scale in the correct way around the avoided crossing as the problem grows.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author generalisation of a result in reference [42], stated without a formal proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that a phase flip applied to the start state at the point where f is zero gives the marked state with unit probability.
quotes: A special case is where this operation is performed on state |ω˜⟩ at the point where f = 0. This will result in the state |m⟩ with unit probability.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without derivation in the main text; the authors point to Appendix D for the Zeno derivation.

assertions.value: The authors report that multiple phase rotations tend to show a Zeno effect, seen as an approach to unit marked state probability, but that the success probability is far from monotonic in the number of phase rotation operations.
quotes: multiple phase rotations tend to illustrate a Zeno effect (as seen by the approach to unit marked state probability), but the dependence of the success probability on the number of phase rotation operations is far from monotonic.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from numerical plots in the idealised model.

assertions.value: The authors state that a projective measurement in the energy eigenbasis exactly at the avoided crossing gives a 50% chance of finding the marked state, and that a measurement anywhere near the crossing gives a non-zero probability.
quotes: Therefore, a measurement in this basis will result in a 50% chance of finding the marked state.
measuring anywhere near the avoided
crossing will result in a non-zero probability of |m⟩.
assertions.certainty_reason: A direct calculation in the two-state model, restated from reference [52]; the value is stated in the paper without a theorem.

assertions.value: The authors derive a lower bound on the probability of the marked state in terms of the purity of the density matrix. They argue that a projective measurement can only decrease the purity and so cannot decrease the lower bound, so sequential measurements cannot cancel exactly.
assertions.anchor: Section 4.1, p.10, and Appendix D.1, pp.25-26
quotes: Since a projective measurement can only decrease Tr ρ2 it cannot decrease the lower bound of ⟨m|ρ|m⟩.
Therefore, unlike in the case of dynamical evolution, there can be no exact cancellation from sequential measurements.
this formula gives a non-zero lower bound on the value of pm
assertions.certainty_reason: The printed bound is garbled in the text layer, so its exact statement and conditions could not be quoted.
assertions.reader_inference: The bound is derived for a two-dimensional density matrix; the proof is in Appendix D.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that the purity argument does not strictly apply to a Zeno effect, because in that case the measurements do not significantly decrease the purity. They then show the Zeno regime numerically and analytically instead.
quotes: An astute reader will notice that the arguments in the last paragraph do not strictly apply to a Zeno effect, since in this case the measurements do not significantly decrease the purity.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own argument in Section 4.1.

assertions.value: The authors report that, if an increasing number of projective measurements are made at points set by the optimal adiabatic schedule, the marked state probability tends to unity.
quotes: Figure 5 illustrates (as filled circles) that indeed if an increasing number of measurements are performed at points determined by the optimal adiabatic schedule, the marked state probability tends to unity.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from numerical plots in the idealised model.

assertions.value: The authors state that a large but finite number of projective measurements gives a valid algorithm but has no well-defined continuum limit, because the total runtime would approach infinity.
quotes: Performing a large but not strictly infinite number of measurements yields a valid algorithm, however this will not have a well-defined continuum limit, since the total runtime will approach infinity.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of discrete measurement protocols.

assertions.value: The authors model decoherence by a coin flip: on heads the system evolves forward under the two-level Hamiltonian, on tails it evolves backward. They state that summing the two density matrices gives decoherence with a rotation angle set by the scaled gap, and that total dephasing with rotation angle π/2 is identical to projective measurement.
quotes: Consider a case where instead of just evolving with the Hamiltonian in equation 8, we instead flip a coin, if it is heads we apply
Summing the density matrices resulting from these two classical choices yields decoherence of the
with ϕ = π/2 is identical to projective measurement.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own decoherence model in Section 4.2.

assertions.value: The authors show that the naive continuum limit of this decoherence, many vanishingly short applications, makes the decoherence vanish. They attribute this to an unintended Zeno effect from frequent reversals of the time evolution.
quotes: In other words, in the continuum limit, the decoherence vanishes if defined in this way.
The reason for the somewhat counter-intuitive behaviour of this limit is actually an unintended Zeno effect
assertions.certainty_reason: Shown by a limit calculation and a numerical illustration in an idealised model.

assertions.value: The authors state a remedy: make reversals less probable per step in proportion to inverse m, so that on average q flips occur independent of m. A large but finite q then approximates continuous decoherence.
quotes: then on average q flips will occur, but this will not scale with m
so therefore we can set q large enough to achieve a good approximation of continuous decoherence
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction justified by an average-case argument, not a theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the effective decoherence coupling rate is finite and independent of the minimum gap and so of system size N. They state the continuous decoherence obeys a Lindblad equation with operator Z̃ = |g⟩⟨g| − |e⟩⟨e|.
quotes: The key aspect of this coupling for our purposes is that it is finite and independent of gmin and
therefore the system size N .
Continuous decoherence in a two state system can be described by a Lindblad equation with a Lindblad operator of
assertions.certainty_reason: A derived rate in an approximate model; the exact equation is garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the derivation of the decoherence master equation assumes q much larger than one, and that the change in f is small over each range. They state it also assumes many reversals have already occurred, and argue this holds because the early states are close to the uniform superposition and the marked state.
quotes: We can then make an approximation based on the fact that q ≫ 1, we assume that the change in f (τj) is not large over the range of j
An astute reader may be concerned that this derivation assumes that many X˜ operations have already occurred.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the approximations its derivation relies on.

assertions.value: The authors report that a continuous Zeno effect from decoherence leads to a success probability that approaches 100%.
quotes: Figure 7 shows that a continuous Zeno effect does indeed lead to success probability which approaches 100%.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from a numerical plot in the idealised model.
assertions.reader_inference: The Figure 7 caption says dissipation and equation 28 although the text ties it to decoherence; likely a caption slip.

assertions.value: The authors state that a partially destructive measurement at the avoided crossing sends the system to the destroyed state 50% of the time, and that the overall success probability is 25% per run, which is still of order one.
quotes: A partially destructive measurement of this type right at the avoided crossing would result in the |d⟩ state 50% of the time, but would be found in the |g⟩ state the other 50%,
and of these cases a subsequent measurement would find |m⟩ 50% of the time, for an overall success probability of 25% each time the algorithm is run.
assertions.certainty_reason: A direct calculation in the idealised two-state model.

assertions.value: The authors state that the purity argument does not hold for destructive measurements because excited-state amplitude is lost. They note that two sequential measurements at the same large gamma magnitude but opposite sign would leave the system completely in the destroyed state.
quotes: this case does not have the elegant argument about purity which could be made in the projective case.
will result in the system being found completely in the |d⟩ state since |e⟩ with γ would be |g⟩ with −γ and vice versa.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of the destruction family.

assertions.value: The authors report that, as the number of partially destructive measurements increases, the success probability can approach 100%.
quotes: Zeno effects are however still possible, and indeed as the number of measurements are increased can approach 100% success, as can be seen in figure 8.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from a numerical plot in the idealised model.

assertions.value: The authors build dissipation from a von Neumann measurement model with a continuous variable and an extra qubit. The qubit is measured and the run aborts, which they equate to moving to the destroyed state, if it reads one. They state this happens only if the system started in the excited state, and then with probability sine squared of twice trot times xmag.
quotes: To perform dissipation, we can then measure the qubit and abort the computation (equivalent to going to a useless state |d⟩) if we measure in the state |1⟩
this only happens if the system started in state |e⟩, and then only with probability sin2 (2trotxmag).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own dissipation model and the resulting abort probability.

assertions.value: The authors state that the von Neumann measurement model can be compiled to a universal quantum computer, where it corresponds to phase estimation, and conclude that it can be considered physically realistic.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2, p.15, and Appendix A, p.22
quotes: As was discussed in [52] this model can be compiled to a universal quantum computer, and in fact corresponds to the well known phase estimation algorithm in that case.
it is clear that this model can be considered physically realistic.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author argument by reference to prior work, not a proof of hardware realisability.

assertions.value: The authors state that naive rescaling of the dissipation model would give a runtime faster than the Grover square-root-of-N scaling, but that it is unphysical. They state that the width of the continuous variable would have to shrink too, and without that the wavepackets would overlap so excited and ground states could not be reliably distinguished.
quotes: the final wavepackets would increasingly overlap as N scales.
it would not be possible to reliably distinguish |e⟩ from |g⟩.
In the actual model we have considered, the final difference in the continuum variable values does not scale with N , therefore the same “sufficiently narrow” width could work for all N values.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this physical limit on the scaling of its own model.

assertions.value: The authors state that dividing the dissipation into q segments with q going to infinity stops the dynamics unless tscale grows with q, because of another Zeno effect from measuring the rotated qubit more often. They state a remedy: omit the measurement within each block so amplitude builds up in the qubit one state, with q large but finite.
quotes: Therefore, if we divide the evolution into q segments with q → ∞, no dynamics will happen unless we also scale tscale ∝ q. The reason for this is actually another Zeno effect.
This strategy can allow amplitude to build up in the |1⟩ state but avoids the unintended Zeno effect.
assertions.certainty_reason: A construction justified by an argument and a numerical illustration, not a theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dissipation in the continuum limit obeys a Lindblad master equation with operator |d⟩⟨e|. They state that, with all dependence on N removed, any evolution with a finite overlap with the marked state is an algorithm with an optimal speedup.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2, p.18, and Appendix E.2, pp.29-30
quotes: Since the action of sending |e⟩ → |d⟩ can be represented as a Lindblad master equation with a Lindblad operator of L = |d⟩⟨e|
As all dependence on N has been removed from this scaled differential equation, any evolution resulting in a finite overlap with |m⟩ corresponds to an algorithm which yields an optimal speedup
assertions.certainty_reason: A derived master equation in an approximate model; the final equation is garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors show a plot of the probability of finding the marked state against total scaled runtime for a Zeno effect from continuous dissipation, modelled by their master equation for destruction.
quotes: Probability of finding the marked state versus total scaled runtime for a Zeno effect due to continuous dissipation, modelled by equation 40.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from a numerical plot; the success probability values are in the figure and not in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that if the measured qubit is reset and the computation continues, instead of aborting, the procedure corresponds to a Zeno effect through weak measurement with the same action as the decoherence studied earlier.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2, p.18, and Appendix F, p.30
quotes: this would correspond to a Zeno effect through weak measurement which would have identical action to the decoherence examined previously
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in Section 5.2 and derived in Appendix F, without a numerical check in the main text.

assertions.value: The authors state that all numerical work used Python with numpy and scipy, and that the hypercube figure used a symmetric subspace with a Hamiltonian matrix of size 21x21. They state the single avoided crossing calculations used exact expressions for eigenvectors and eigenvalues.
quotes: All numerical calculations were performed using Python, making use of numpy [59] for simple matrix operations, and scipy[60]
a symmetric subspace was used, so the Hamiltonian matrix was of size 21x21
For all single avoided crossing calculations, the exact expressions for eigenvectors and eigenvalues were used
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own numerical setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that each of the three families has three manifestations and that all of them can yield optimal speedup for unstructured search.
quotes: In each of the three families of Zeno effects we have studied, we have found three manifestations of the effect, which can all
yield optimal speedup for unstructured search.
assertions.certainty_reason: A summary of arguments and numerics in an idealised model.

assertions.value: The authors state that all nine combinations of families and manifestations will have algorithms with optimal scaling that do not show Zeno effects, and cite search by measurement and a single continuous-time quantum walk as existing examples.
quotes: all nine combinations of families and manifestations will have algorithms with optimal scaling but which do not illustrate Zeno effects
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim from the scaling arguments, without separate demonstration for each combination.

assertions.value: The authors report from their figures that the phase rotation family has the most favourable constant factors, followed by decoherence, then destruction. They state it is not clear whether this ordering carries over to structured optimisation problems.
quotes: We find that the phase rotation family has the most favourable constant factors, followed by decoherence, followed by destruction.
it is not clear whether or not these factors would translate to structured (optimisation) problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical comparison from simplified-model plots.

assertions.value: The authors state that they did not examine finite-size effects, as was done in reference [42], and did not study how the mechanisms interact with each other. They state that the models are more complicated to implement than a direct unstructured search Hamiltonian.
quotes: we have not examined the effect of finite size on our algorithm as was done in [42].
We have further not studied how the mechanisms interact with each other.
all the Hamiltonians we have discussed here would be more complicated to implement than directly implementing an unstructured search Hamiltonian
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states these limits of its own scope in Section 7.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not discuss how to encode a problem into the entropy-computing paradigm, and that how such a device could be achieved is beyond the scope of the work.
quotes: Note that we will not discuss how to actually encode the problem to this paradigm, as that is beyond the scope of this current work.
Discussing how such a device could actually be achieved is beyond the scope of this work
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states these exclusions from its own scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that many coherent Ising machine implementations use classical feedback that destroys meaningful quantum superposition, and that one would then expect classical scaling for unstructured search. They state the currently implemented entropy computers use such feedback, and that both paradigms can incorporate quantum search if implemented all-optically.
quotes: many implementations of coherent Ising machines are based on classical feedback which destroys meaningful quantum superposition [17] in this case one would expect the classical scaling for unstructured search.
Similarly the currently implemented entropy computers use such feedback [12].
Both paradigms however can incorporate quantum search if implemented in an all-optical way [12, 16].
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement with cited support and no new evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: This caveat applies to the existing hardware: the speedup results in this paper do not describe machines that use classical feedback.

assertions.value: The authors describe entropy computing as an optical paradigm that can support a fully quantum implementation, and say it has shown promising results in early experiments that use classical electronics for feedback [12].
quotes: Entropy computing is an optical paradigm which can support a fully quantum implementation and has demonstrated promising results in early experiments which make use of classical electronics for feedback [12].
assertions.certainty_reason: A company-affiliated authors' description of their own employer's paradigm; the authors state that all were supported by Quantum Computing Inc.

assertions.value: The authors use a damped-oscillator equation for a model of Zeno blockade with loss. They state the underdamped regime resembles the phase rotation manifestation and the overdamped regime resembles the destruction manifestation, and that these map roughly to coherent and incoherent quantum Zeno blockade regimes.
quotes: If we assume that an effective Zeno blockade is implemented, then terms proportional to c can be neglected, leading to an overall combined differential equation of
These regimes roughly map to the coherent (CQZ) and incoherent (IQZ) quantum Zeno blockade regimes
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualitative mapping in a simplified model; the damping condition is garbled in the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The mapping links the paper's abstract families to the entropy computing hardware of the authors' employer; no experiment is shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that the single avoided crossing model loses information about constant factors away from the asymptotic limit, and that this is not a major drawback because the aim is to argue that speedups exist, not to compare models.
quotes: A minor disadvantage of the single avoided crossing model is that it loses information about constant factors away from the asymptotic limit
Since the purpose of our current work is to argue the existence of speedups, not to compare models, this is not a major drawback.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of its own model.

assertions.value: The authors show the spectrum of the qubit hypercube search Hamiltonian for n equal to 20 and state this size already strongly shows the single avoided crossing limit.
quotes: figure 10 shows the spectrum of the (qubit) hypercube Hamiltonian for n = 20, a size which already strongly shows the limiting behaviour.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one numerical diagonalisation.

assertions.value: The authors cite reference [39] for the result that, for quantum walks, a Grover speedup is possible for hypercubes of dimension four and greater, with an optimal speedup for dimension above four. They state the result extends to qudits except for three or fewer qudits, and that a fixed number of qudits is not a valid route to scalable computation.
quotes: it has been shown that a Grover speedup is possible for hypercubes of dimension four and greater (n ≥ 4 in our notation), with an optimal speedup for n > 4 [39] and d ≥ 2.
Computing with a fixed number of qudits does not represent a valid way to perform scalable quantum computing [74]
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result; the paper does not re-prove it.

assertions.value: The authors state that an earlier paper by Childs and co-authors showed a single measurement can be done in a time proportional to the square root of N, with an O(1) success probability independent of system size, so an algorithm based on single measurements can match Grover scaling.
quotes: The measurement time combined with the fact that after this measurement there is an O(1) success probability independent of system size, implies that an algorithm based on single measurements is theoretically able to achieve the same scaling as Grover’s famous gate model algorithm [36, 37].
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result from Childs et al. (reference 52).

assertions.value: The authors state that, in the von Neumann measurement model with a fixed position precision, the required measurement time depends inversely on the difference in eigenvalues of the measured operator, which is the energy gap when that operator is a Hamiltonian.
quotes: in other words, it will depend inversely on the difference in expectation values of Aˆ, which is the energy gap in the case where Aˆ is a Hamiltonian5.
assertions.certainty_reason: A short model derivation restated from prior work; the equation is garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors derive that, with an energy-basis measurement at each step starting in the ground state, the excited-state population accumulates only second-order terms in the small basis change per step, so a Zeno effect maintains the instantaneous ground state. They state the same holds with removal of the excited state, and for rapid continuous dissipation or decoherence.
quotes: This illustrates the presence of a Zeno effect, which maintains the instantaneous ground state since ρee +ρgg = 1 by definition.
These arguments apply equally to rapid continuous dissipation or decoherence.
assertions.certainty_reason: A first-order perturbative derivation without an explicit bound statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that the optimal adiabatic schedule can be related to the Gauss-Bonnet theorem near the anti-crossing [75]. They suggest this gives a differential geometry description of the Zeno manifestations and leave it for future work.
quotes: adiabatic schedule can be related to the Gauss-Bonnet theorem in the vicinity of the anti-crossing [75].
We leave this for future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited connection with no derivation in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors cite reference [27] for a demonstration that a non-unitary Zeno effect implemented through measurement can give a Grover-type advantage, and describe it as a specific example of the more general result of this paper.
quotes: In [27] it was even demonstrated that a non-unitary Zeno effect implemented through measurement can be used to obtain a Grover-type advantage, a specific example of the more general result we show here.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited result from Pyshkin et al.

assertions.value: The authors state that decoherence can be modelled by replacing the post-selection in the dissipation model with a step that resets the extra qubit, and that the effect on the system is to reduce the off-diagonal elements of its density matrix.
quotes: and the effect of the operation is to reduce the off-diagonal elements of ρsys.
assertions.certainty_reason: A derivation shown in outline; no numerical check is given for this alternative model.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that analog quantum computation where many-body manifestations of these effects are present can also support a quantum advantage, and that such specialised devices are likely to be easier to build in the near term in analogy to quantum annealing.
quotes: What we have shown is that analog quantum computation where a many-body manifestations of the effects are present can also support a quantum advantage.
Such specialized devices are likely to be easier to build in the near term
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion; the near-term buildability claim has no evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The speedup is shown only for unstructured search in a two-state model; the near-term device claim is a prediction.
